chunks.text: The pygmy date palm is a small, slow-growing, single- or multi-stemmed palm native to a fairly narrow strip of southeastern Asia — southwestern China's Yunnan province, northern Laos and the northern Vietnamese provinces of Dien Bien, Ha Giang, Cao Bang and Lang Son — where it tends to grow along fast-flowing rivers. Mature plants usually stand somewhere between 2 and 7 metres tall, bearing pinnate leaves 60–120 cm long made up of around 100 narrow, grey-green leaflets roughly 15–25 cm long that droop slightly and lie arranged in a single plane, a detail botanists use to distinguish it from the closely related Phoenix loureiroi. Small yellowish flowers appear on a short inflorescence, and because the species is dioecious, only female plants go on to produce the fruit: a small, roughly 1 cm drupe that looks like a miniature, thin-fleshed date and is, in fact, edible, even if rarely eaten in practice. The specific name honours the orchid collector Carl Roebelen. Commercially it is valued almost entirely as an ornamental — it needs little pruning, shrugs off most pests, and has been awarded the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit — and it was one of the species tested in NASA's Clean Air Study, which found it effective at removing indoor air pollutants such as formaldehyde and benzene, a finding often cited in support of its popularity as a houseplant.

chunks.source: NC State Extension — Phoenix roebelenii (Robellini Palm) Plant Toolbox
chunks.text: NC State's Extension plant database fills in practical growing details that complement the botanical picture: outdoors the palm tends to reach about 6.5 feet, a bit less indoors, and while it clusters naturally in the wild, cultivated specimens are usually single-stemmed, so growers often pot three or five young palms together to mimic a fuller, clumping look. It tolerates full sun to partial shade but benefits from protection against harsh afternoon sun, prefers soil kept lightly moist without becoming waterlogged (overwatering risks root rot), and is rated hardy only in USDA zones 10a–11b, which is why it is grown as a container or houseplant well outside the true tropics. An important handling note: the lowest leaflets on each frond are modified into sharp spines, so the extension service explicitly warns to use caution when pruning or handling the foliage. The palm is tolerant of heat, humidity and drought once established, grows slowly, and is low-maintenance, though it can suffer from scale insects, leaf spot and thrips. Usefully for anyone with pets, the listing tags it as non-toxic to cats, dogs and horses, and notes that in the trade it is sometimes confused with Chamaedorea species or Cycas revoluta — a reminder that 'palm-like' houseplants are not always true palms.
